findings.passage: "if I was singing to one person, I would like be sweating profusely. But like thousands of people, it's easier."
findings.problem: One word of this direct quotation rests on the caption track alone. The draft stage's second machine transcription rendered it "sweating for music"; my third, a larger model on freshly downloaded audio, has "I would like be sweating." with no adverb. The sense is confirmed by all three and the caption reading is probably right, but no person has listened. The article does disclose that video quotations were not checked by ear.
findings.acceptance_test: Before publication, a person listens at about 03:13 of the Snapchat video and confirms "profusely", or the quotation is cut back to words all three transcriptions share (for example, she said she would be sweating in front of one person, "But like thousands of people, it's easier."). C48 records which was done.

findings.passage: Her answer, in The Line of Best Fit: "I'm such a Noah Kahan fan," and "I'm not out here trying to interpolate other people's songs."
findings.problem: The interview ran on July 3, 2026. The sentence before it reports criticism dated September 2, 2026, so "Her answer" reads as a reply to critics who cite her old covers. She said this two months earlier, about commenters who heard the likeness. Both quotations are exact; only the implied order is off.
findings.acceptance_test: The sentence shows the order, for example "She had already told The Line of Best Fit in July:", and nothing implies she has replied to the cover-video criticism.

findings.passage: By May there were advisers, who told her to avoid country "because I wasn't from the South,"
findings.problem: In SongwriterUniverse, Virgin Radio and Vanity Fair her word is "people" ("a lot of voices in my head of people telling me"). "Advisers" suggests identified professionals, and no source says who they were; the evidence record itself lists that as unexplained.
findings.acceptance_test: The first mention uses her word ("By May there were people telling her to avoid country"), or says that she does not identify them. "Advised" stays for the tour post, where it is her word.

findings.passage: As of October 11, 2026, the people quoted describing her firsthand all worked with her, toured with her or were dating her that year.
findings.problem: This is true of the sources opened, but the sentence is written as a statement about all coverage, and two relevant pieces (The Washington Post, People) were not opened. Elsewhere the article limits such statements to "the sources opened for this profile".
findings.acceptance_test: The sentence carries the same limit ("in the sources opened for this profile"), and C30 matches it exactly.

evidence.reason: I reopened all 27 sources behind the final claims (25 live, two in archive captures) and traced all 75 quoted strings; every print quotation matches in wording, speaker and context, and writers' words are kept apart from hers ("Rolling Stone's writer says she turned it down"). Interested witnesses are flagged, disputes carry both sides, and limits sit at the point of use. Held below 9 by caption-sourced quotations that no person has heard (one adverb is unconfirmed), two outlet-relayed posts, and three small wording slips (verify-02 to verify-04). The record is thin and the article says so; I found no overreach.

enneagram.reason: Scored against the open-case anchor. Each read is argued from her own dated statements: Nine from the Los Angeles year and the Kahan concession, Six from "I always worried" and "really had me spiraling", Seven from "I will not pick a lane", Three from the smiling take and "TikTok decides". The article names what does not discriminate and what would, and claims no more confidence than the record holds. Short of higher because the lead over Six is admitted to be near a coin toss, the comply-then-reverse pattern has one long instance and one doubtful one, and the "saying yes" frame starts from the Nine description of her behavior.

originality.reason: The insight is specific to her and comes from reading the interviews by date: her account of the Los Angeles year changes from her own pivot in March to other people's direction by May. The smiling-take test, the one-listener fear beside daily posting, and the three versions of the publisher story are details no other profile could reuse. Type boilerplate is limited to four one-line motives.

writing.passage: So the pattern this profile counts runs one way: she complies first and reverses later. The Los Angeles year fits it, at length.
writing.reason: Plain, exact sentences, sections that each add something, and a close that says what stands whichever read wins. The cost of the care is density: the allegations section reads as a ledger, attributions and hedges slow the Type sections, and at about 3,000 words the piece runs past the open-case target of roughly 1,200 to 2,500. Nothing is padding, but the middle sags.

durability.passage: As of October 11, 2026, two changes have no first-person account: the end of her opening slot on Wetmore's tour, and a split from her managers that Billboard reported on September 27, 2026, citing unnamed sources, and that no party has confirmed.
durability.reason: Scored against the open-case anchor. Every changing fact carries an absolute date or an as-of date, each time-sensitive claim has a trigger, and the three settle signals plus the 2026-12-01 review date (with a stated fallback) make the page easy to reopen. The hook and the pattern rest on 2024 and 2025 episodes, and the closing paragraph would stay true if a later run settled on Six, Seven or Three. I set the five-year flag to false because an open case is provisional by design and schedules its own reopening; that does not block release in this format. One present-tense status (her older posts being offline) rests on a September report.
